## Publications

Publications appear in reverse chronological order.

### Exploring Brain Activity in Novice Athletes During Closed and Open Skills in Table Tennis

Zack Murphy, Jennifer Kemp, and David Vandenheever. *Journal of Motor Behavior*, 1–12, 2026.<br>
[Free publisher access](https://www.tandfonline.com/eprint/RDNADAIYPQBX9WHNJYN5/full?target=10.1080/00222895.2026.2691791){target="_blank"} | [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1080/00222895.2026.2691791){target="_blank"} | [Download accepted manuscript (PDF)](assets/publications/murphy-et-al-2026-table-tennis-accepted-manuscript.pdf){download=""} | [BibTeX](assets/publications/murphy-et-al-2026-table-tennis.bib){download=""}

This study used EEG to compare preparatory brain activity during closed-skill serves and open-skill returns in novice table tennis players. Task- and performance-related differences in alpha, beta, and theta power suggest distinct neural demands across the two skills and potential targets for motor-skill training.

### Exploring facial expression processing with fast periodic visual stimulation and diverse stimuli

David Vandenheever, Haleigh Davidson, Jennifer Kemp, Zack Murphy, Autumn Kujawa, Jingyi Shi, Michael R. Nadorff, Kayla Bates-Brantley, and MacKenzie Sidwell. *Brain and Cognition*, 189, 106338, 2025.
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bandc.2025.106338){target="_blank"} | [ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0278262625000788){target="_blank"}

This study used FPVS and EEG to examine facial expression processing with diverse, naturalistic stimuli. Robust expression-related neural responses were observed, supporting FPVS as a sensitive framework for studying emotional face processing.

### Preliminary evidence for anxiety-linked neural sensitivity to emotional faces using fast periodic visual stimulation

David Vandenheever, Haleigh Davidson, Jennifer Kemp, Zack Murphy, Autumn Kujawa, Jingyi Shi, Michael R. Nadorff, Kayla Bates-Brantley, and MacKenzie Sidwell. *International Journal of Psychophysiology*, 2025.
[DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijpsycho.2025.113212){target="_blank"} | [ScienceDirect](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167876025007081){target="_blank"} | [OSF data and analysis scripts](https://osf.io/5xkae/files/osfstorage){target="_blank"}

This study used Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation (FPVS) and EEG to test whether anxiety-linked characteristics are associated with differences in neural responses to emotional facial expressions. Participants with anxiety-related characteristics showed stronger occipital responses to angry and sad faces, providing preliminary evidence that FPVS may capture trait-level differences in emotional face processing.
